The first thing my father did after retiring was move the kitchen clock six inches to the left. It had hung above the telephone for thirty years, but the telephone was gone, and from his new chair at the table he could see only half its face behind the lampshade. He measured the distance, made a pencil mark, and fetched his drill. At lunch my mother came home and said, “Who moved the clock?” She had not yet put down her bag. This struck him as an extraordinary tribute to the precision with which she observed the world.

What she had actually noticed was the pale circle on the wall. Everywhere else, the yellow paint had deepened under successive summers of frying onions, boiling peaches, and occasionally setting a dish towel on fire. Behind the clock was a patch of innocent lemon. My father proposed washing the wall. My mother proposed putting the clock back. They compromised by doing nothing for eleven years. Whenever I visited, I meant to ask whether the circle bothered them anymore. Whenever I left, I remembered that I had forgotten to ask. Eventually the circle became the thing I looked for when I came in.

My parents sold the house in February. The woman who bought it was a piano teacher named June, who asked if she might keep the curtains until she could afford new ones. My mother left her the curtains, the rods, a stepladder, and a note explaining which neighbors would lend her what. Mr. Bello had a long extension cord. The twins next door owned a wheelbarrow, although you had to inflate the tire. Nobody had a decent posthole digger. The note ran to three pages and did not mention that the upstairs bathroom door could lock itself in damp weather.

I went back in April for a box of records we had overlooked in the attic. June answered in stocking feet, holding a spoon. Somewhere beyond her a child was playing the same four notes over and over, with a long investigative pause between the third and fourth. She led me through the kitchen. Both circles were still there: the pale one and, six inches to its left, the cleaner ring left by the clock when my father took it down. June had drawn two black dots and a smile inside the first. Inside the second she had drawn a frown.

“Reviews,” she said, lifting the spoon toward the piano. The child landed hard on a fifth note, an event so unexpected that we stood still to hear what he would do about it. He played it again, softly. Then he began working his way backward, trying to find the four notes by which he had arrived. June waited until he found them before calling out, “Good, Milo. Now come have some soup.” I had assumed the spoon was for conducting. This is one difficulty with returning to a familiar house: you expect everything new in it to require an explanation.

In the attic I found the records beneath a quilt that did not belong to us. June had already begun storing things up there. A carton marked CHRISTMAS contained, as far as I could see through the open flaps, a single red mitten and an astonishing quantity of wire. Beside it stood a plaster foot, larger than an ordinary foot, with each toenail painted blue. I wanted badly to know its history and understood that I no longer possessed the right to shout down the stairs and ask. I took the records and left the foot to its private business.

At their apartment my father was setting up the turntable. He had chosen the place partly because its living room accommodated his speakers at what he considered the correct distance from one another. This left my mother very little choice about where to put the sofa, but in exchange she had an entire small bedroom for sewing. For years she had cut patterns on the dining table, clearing everything away before supper. Now she could leave a sleeve unfinished on Tuesday and find it precisely as unfinished on Friday. Nothing about retirement, she told me, had equaled this particular luxury.

We played a recording of a clarinet concerto. Halfway through, my father got up and moved the right speaker an inch. My mother looked up from the cuff she was hemming. “Better,” she said. I could hear no difference. Then a delivery truck outside reversed, contributing three evenly spaced beeps in a key surprisingly hospitable to the orchestra. My father laughed so hard he had to lift the needle. We ate sandwiches. For dessert my mother produced two pears, which she divided among the three of us by a system whose fairness she defended before anybody had thought to object.

I told them about the faces June had drawn on the kitchen wall. My mother immediately wanted to know which face was smiling, the original position or the revised one. My father said this was not a competition. When I told them it was the original position, he said that a piano teacher was hardly the person to consult about the placement of a clock. He went to the window with his plate and stood eating the last sliver of pear. Across the street, someone had hung bright green curtains in a room otherwise empty except for a bicycle.

Before I left, I noticed their clock on the sill beside his elbow. There were no holes in the apartment walls yet. “Where will you put that?” I asked. He turned it around so the face pointed out the window. We considered the arrangement. From our side all you could see was a battery compartment and a little brass wheel. My mother joined us. Across the street a young man came into the room with the green curtains, unlocked his bicycle from the radiator, and glanced our way. My father raised his hand. The young man checked his wrist and waved.
